item.title: Britecharts 3.0 beta 8, accessible by default
item.description: Britecharts 3.0.0-beta.8 is out! Every chart in it can be read by a screen reader cell by cell, used with a keyboard, themed with CSS and drawn in dark mode, with no setup. It is also the first version built for coding agents as well as for people.
item.content:encoded:
Britecharts 3.0.0-beta.8 is out! Every chart in it can be read by a screen reader cell by cell, used with a keyboard, themed with CSS and drawn in dark mode, with no setup. It is also the first version built for coding agents as well as for people.

npm install @britecharts/core@beta

Why there is another beta​

I wrote that beta 7 would be the last beta, and that only bug fixes would come before 3.0.0. That did not happen. I compared Britecharts with eight current charting libraries, and the comparison showed what Britecharts can do better than any of them: finished charts that are accessible by default, free, and easy for an agent to write. Most of that work changes the API, so it had to land before 3.0.0 fixes the API in place.

Accessible by default​

Only one library in that comparison gave readers a data table, keyboard navigation and reduced motion together, and it charges per seat. Every Britecharts chart now does all of it, with each part on by default and each one possible to turn off. See how to make a chart accessible.

  • Its data as a table. Every chart but the legend renders its data as a visually hidden table after its svg, so a screen reader can read it cell by cell. Series charts lay it out with a row per date or name and a column per series. Turn it off with a11yDataTable(false).
  • A keyboard can move through the data. The bar, donut, grouped bar, heatmap, line, scatter plot, stacked area and stacked bar charts are each one tab stop. The arrow keys move between points, Home and End go to the ends, and Escape lets go. The point is highlighted and the tooltip follows focus, as they do for a pointer. Turn it off with a11yKeyboardNavigation(false).
  • Still when the reader asks. With prefers-reduced-motion, the charts draw without animation whatever isAnimated says, and the tooltip and legend stop fading.
  • A colour-blind-safe palette. colors.colorSchemas.okabeIto keeps its eight colours apart with the common kinds of colour blindness.

Themes and dark mode, with CSS​

Every colour around the data is now a --bc-* custom property: text, axes, grid, tooltips, legend and loading states. The charts follow your page's color-scheme through light-dark(), so color-scheme: light dark on your page is all dark mode needs. To change one colour, set its token, such as .britechart { --bc-text-muted: #555 }. A page that declares no colour scheme stays light. See how to theme a chart.

Made for coding agents​

An agent writes a chart correctly more often when the library tells it what it needs. This beta adds four ways to do that:

  • An agent skill ships in @britecharts/core, with each chart's data shape, accessors, events and the v2 code that no longer works. Install it with npx skills add britecharts/britecharts.
  • A JSON Schema for every chart's spec, { chart, config, data }, generated from the TypeScript types and published at https://britecharts.github.io/britecharts/schema/v3/<chart>.json. An editor or an agent can check a spec before drawing it. See how to describe a chart as a spec.
  • Errors that say how to fix them. A misspelt key gets heigth: did you mean height? and a link to the chart's API page. A value of the wrong type names the type it should be.
  • llms.txt describes every chart and accessor, generated from the same comments as the API pages.

New in the charts​

  • 100% stacks. isNormalized(true) stretches every stack of the stacked bar, or every date of the stacked area, to fill the value axis, which then reads from 0% to 100%.
  • Any categories in the heatmap. xAxisLabels joins yAxisLabels, so a heatmap can compare any two sets of categories, such as a square grid of six.
  • SVG export. exportChart('chart.svg') downloads an svg with its styles inlined, so it looks the same outside the page and stays sharp at any size.
  • Every chart in every package. The brush and the heatmap now have a wrapper and a React component, like the other charts.
  • Fixes you may have hit. The brush no longer flickers on a second selection or fires customBrushEnd while idle. The animated stacked bar grows each stack as one block. The legend's highlight commands no longer throw before it draws. A bullet can have more than one marker.
  • Smaller app bundles. Each package declares sideEffects, so bundlers can drop the charts an app does not import. In a bar-only test app, the bundle went from 104.0 kB to 89.6 kB.

The Storybook shows all of it, with the same stories under the same names in core and in React.

What to check before you upgrade​

Five changes in this beta can affect a page that works with beta 7:

  1. Charts add a tab stop and a hidden table. If your page has its own table of the same data, or a tab order to keep, turn them off with a11yDataTable(false) or a11yKeyboardNavigation(false).
  2. The wrappers check value types. create and update throw on a value of the wrong type, such as height: "300". Before, the string reached the chart.
  3. An exported title gets its own band. The title sits in a 30px band above the chart instead of over its top edge, so an exported image with a title is 30px taller.
  4. The heatmap's label classes changed. .day-label is now .row-label, .hour-label is .column-label, and their groups are .row-labels-group and .column-labels-group. The row labels now end at the grid, and both axes share one label style.
  5. Some colours are set as styles now. The tooltip's text, the donut's empty slice, the scatter plot's hollow circles, the line chart's custom lines, the sparkline's gradient and the heatmap's labels take their colours from the --bc-* tokens, set on the element. A CSS rule on those elements no longer wins, so set the token instead.

If you are coming from version 2, the migration guide has the full list.

What happens next​

The API work I wanted before 3.0.0 is done, so this time I mean it: what follows is bug fixes, then 3.0.0. Bigger features, such as server-side rendering, a Canvas renderer or Web Component bindings, wait as issues that need votes. Add a 👍 to the ones you would use.

Please try this beta in a real project, with a screen reader and a keyboard if you can. Open an issue with the chart, the data and what you expected.

Britecharts still needs maintainers. If you would like to own part of it, the contributing guide is where to start.

item.title: Britecharts 3.0 beta 7, the last beta
item.description: Britecharts 3.0.0-beta.7 is out, and it is the last beta. The next release I plan to publish is 3.0.0 itself. Test against this version if you want your bug fixed before the stable release rather than after it.
item.content:encoded:
Britecharts 3.0.0-beta.7 is out, and it is the last beta. The next release I plan to publish is 3.0.0 itself. Test against this version if you want your bug fixed before the stable release rather than after it.

npm install @britecharts/core@beta

What changed since the first beta​

When I announced the beta in September, I said it held more than a version bump. The betas since then have made the packages behave the way modern tooling expects. They also fixed the places where the charts said one thing and did another. Here is what you will notice:

  • One bundle per package, built with Vite. Version 2 published a file for every chart. Version 3 now publishes one UMD bundle and one CDN bundle per package, plus ES modules for bundlers. Bundlers already drop the charts you do not import, so a file per chart saved nothing there. On a page with a script tag, one request is better than five.
  • Real ES module packages. The three packages declare "type": "module", so import works in Node as well as in bundlers, with matching types for each way of loading. require still works and loads the CommonJS bundle, which now ends in .cjs.
  • Charts that screen readers can name. Every chart gives its svg a role and an accessible name, "Bar chart" by default. Set a11yTitle to name it after what it shows. Set a11yDescription to add a sentence about what it means.
  • Negative values in the scatter plot. Its value axis now runs below zero when the data does, and each circle's size shows the size of its value. That completes the negative values work: the bar, grouped bar, stacked bar, brush and scatter plot charts all draw them.
  • Typings that match the charts. I compared every chart's published types with what it does at run time, and fixed more than a hundred mismatches. Getters were declared as setters, callbacks had the wrong return type, and accessors were declared but never existed. If TypeScript accepts a call now, the chart does what the call says.
  • Smaller fixes you may have hit. The brush honours locale and the stacked area honours numberFormat, which both used to do nothing. The scatter plot's zoom works again. The grouped and stacked bar tooltips no longer flicker when you move across the bars. Resting the pointer on a chart no longer pops up the browser's own tooltip. A chart's valueLocale no longer changes the numbers of every other chart on the page. A colorMap that names only some categories colours the rest from the palette.
  • Tooltips that say what each chart needs. The charts name the fields of the data they send the tooltip differently. Some of them need the tooltip told where to look: topicLabel('values') for the stacked area, nameLabel('stack') or nameLabel('group') for the stacked and grouped bars, valueLabel('y') for the scatter plot. The tooltip reference and a new how-to list them per chart. Every story shows them in use.
  • Leaner API pages and more recipes. Each accessor's heading starts with its name instead of exports., in the pages and in their tables of contents. The how-to guides gain recipes for per-category colours, number and date formats, loading states, animation, negative values and accessibility.
  • In React, Tooltip infers its data type from its data prop, so its render callback type-checks without a cast. Seven settings the charts always had are now props, and prop-types is no longer a peer dependency.

What to check before you upgrade​

If you tried an earlier beta, five changes in this stretch can break your code. The migration guide covers each of them with a before and after:

  1. Per-chart files are gone. Import the charts from the package, or load dist/cdn/bundle/core.cdn.min.js and use the core global.
  2. CommonJS bundles end in .cjs. This matters only if you required a bundle by its path.
  3. The bullet chart and the sparkline no longer draw titles. Text inside an svg cannot wrap and ignores your page's typography, so put the label in your own markup and pass the same text to a11yTitle.
  4. An accessor you have not set reads null, on every chart. Before, some charts returned undefined. A truthiness check works as before.
  5. The data-key accessors are gone. nameLabel, valueLabel, dateLabel and the rest no longer let a chart read your data under other keys. They had warned since version 2 that they would go. Rename the keys in your data to the ones the chart's data shape names, such as name and value. The tooltip keeps its own four.

If you are coming from version 2, the guide has the full list. Version 2 ends at 2.18.2.

What happens next​

Between now and 3.0.0, I only plan to fix bugs. The API is settled, so if something in it is wrong, now is the last cheap moment to say so. After 3.0.0 ships, changing it means another major version.

So please try this beta in a real project. Open an issue with the chart, the data and what you expected. The Storybook shows every chart and its options, in core and in React. It is the fastest way to check whether something is a bug or a setting.

Britecharts still needs maintainers. If you would like to own part of it, the contributing guide is where to start.

item.title: Britecharts 3.0 beta
item.description: Britecharts 3.0 is in beta. I split it into three packages this time — @britecharts/core for the charts themselves, @britecharts/react for the React components, and @britecharts/wrappers, the layer the React components are built on and, I hope, the seam a Vue or Svelte binding will eventually grow out of.
item.content:encoded:
Britecharts 3.0 is in beta. I split it into three packages this time — @britecharts/core for the charts themselves, @britecharts/react for the React components, and @britecharts/wrappers, the layer the React components are built on and, I hope, the seam a Vue or Svelte binding will eventually grow out of.

npm install @britecharts/core@beta

What is new​

There is more here than a version bump, so let me go through it in the order I think you will actually notice it:

  • Modern modules. Built on the current d3 modules, shipped as ES modules, CommonJS, UMD and CDN builds, with an exports map and TypeScript typings for every chart. Vite, Rollup, esbuild and webpack all work out of the box, which was not true of v2 — every bundler had its own workaround, and I was tired of maintaining them.
  • Smaller bundles. The build now targets ES2020, and Babel is gone entirely from @britecharts/core and @britecharts/wrappers — the core UMD bundle drops 12.7% (151,923 → 132,626 bytes) and the React bundle 14% (368 → 315 KB). You do not need to do anything for this one; a browser below the new target already needs a bundler or its own polyfills to run modern syntax at all, so nothing that worked before stops working now.
  • One tooltip. tooltip and miniTooltip used to be two components with two sets of bugs. They are one now, and it never gets cut off at the chart's edges, follows the pointer smoothly, and behaves the same way whichever chart it is attached to.
  • Negative values on the bar, stacked bar, grouped bar and brush charts, stacking down from zero. This has been the second-most-requested thing since 2019, and the reason it took this long is that I kept underestimating how much of the domain math assumed zero was the floor.
  • Loading states for every chart, colorMap to name the colour of each category, animationDuration on every animated chart, and charts that are responsive by default.
  • React 19 is tested end to end, not just claimed: the unit suite itself now runs on React 19, and the React package is also installed into a real React 19 project under StrictMode on every change. If you have been holding off upgrading because you weren't sure the wrappers would survive StrictMode's double-invoked effects, that is exactly what this checks.

Moving from version 2​

Most of the work is renaming, and I tried to keep it that way on purpose — a rewrite nobody can follow is worse than a major version nobody wants to install. The migration guide walks through every breaking change with a before and after for each. The ones you will hit first:

  1. Imports. The charts are named exports of @britecharts/core (import { bar } from '@britecharts/core') instead of files under britecharts/dist/umd. The CommonJS, UMD and CDN paths are in the guide too.
  2. Loading states. loadingState() is gone; render the chart with isLoading(true) and a dataset, empty or not.
  3. Renamed accessors. locale is valueLocale on the bar, grouped bar, stacked bar and scatter plot; the value formatters of the grouped and stacked bar are numberFormat; the line and stacked area swap xAxisFormat and xAxisCustomFormat back to what their names say; aspectRatio is removed.
  4. Tooltips. The line, stacked area, stacked bar and grouped bar charts now dispatch customMouseMove the same way every other chart does, as (dataPoint, [x, y], [width, height], colorMap). If you drive tooltip.update yourself, it still accepts the old argument order and warns once.
  5. exportChart returns a promise.

Version 2 ends at 2.18.2. I am not going to pretend I will keep patching it once 3.0 ships, so if you are on v2 and this list looks manageable, better to do it now than after a security report forces the question.

Where to start​

  • The installation and getting started tutorials build a first chart from scratch, and styling charts covers themes and CSS.
  • The API reference has a page per chart and one for the tooltip.
  • The Storybook shows every chart, in core and in React, with its options live — that is usually faster than reading accessor names off a page.

Tell us what breaks​

A beta is only useful if people actually try to break it, so please do. Open an issue with the chart, the data and what you expected instead — the more specific, the faster I can act on it.

I will also say plainly what the contributing guide says: Britecharts needs maintainers. I have carried this release mostly on my own, and a 3.7k-star library with one person behind it is not a sustainable place to leave it. If any part of this codebase is something you would enjoy owning, that guide is where to start the conversation.
